At ultrahigh energies, the arrival directions of cosmic rays are expected to reflect the distribution of their sources and are deflected by intergalactic and galactic magnetic fields. Consequently, any detected anisotropy can offer insights into the nature of the source population and the properties of these magnetic fields. Although the energy threshold for observing such anisotropies is relatively modest—roughly one-tenth of the GZK cutoff, which corresponds to proton-proton inelasticity times the diffuse photon background density—itremains challenging to identify the specific sources. At energies where the mean free path for the GZK interaction exceeds the size of any plausible astrophysical source distribution, the resulting directionality may mimic a isotropic field, such as generated by the local supercluster. Moreover, if the mean free path becomes significantly larger than the Hubble distance, the GZK interaction ceases to limit the flux, and the true energies of the observed cosmic rays may extend even further.

Pierre Auger Observatory data have already revealed the onset of anisotropy detection at energies above 6 EeV. While no specific region of the sky has been found to be depleted of events—ruling out a binary scenario of nearby sources and a diffuse background—the increased flux at higher energies suggests a power-law distribution of ultrahigh-energy sources. While the conventional stance holds that table instances must adhere to all imposed functional dependencies, it is equally significant to formulate theories for handling instances that violate certain dependencies. Concerning missing values, we do not presuppose their existence; rather, a missing value is considered to exist only if it can be inferred from the table's functional dependencies.

We present a formal framework where each table tuple is assigned one of four truth values: true, false, inconsistent, or unknown. We demonstrate that this framework facilitates the study of critical issues such as consistent query answering, table merging, and data quality metrics, among others. However, this work primarily concentrates on consistent query answering, a problem that has garnered significant attention over recent decades.

The author's previous efforts in managing missing values through logical theories are highlighted, along with the algorithm developed for addressing this problem. Furthermore, we show how this approach can be adapted to manage missing values in tables without functional dependencies and in tables with partial functional dependencies. Additionally, a formal method for managing missing values in relational algebra queries over tables with functional dependencies is described.

Finally, the proposed method is applied to a real-world scenario involving the merging of two news feeds, demonstrating how the logical theory approach effectively handles missing values and inconsistencies within that context. Title: Generalizing Object Manipulation from Demonstration via Neural Descriptor Fields

Authors: Yilun Du, Maciej Beccue, and Maciej Malisiewicz

Abstract: Achieving successful and generalizable object manipulation from demonstration remains a challenging task. While previous studies have encoded demonstrated poses into 2D descriptors for robot tasks, these approaches often struggle with generalization across 3D poses and object instances, and can be sensitive to background distractions. In this work, we propose representing object poses with 3D descriptors. Specifically, we introduce a neural network that encodes the 3D structure of an object along with several demonstrated poses into a descriptor that is both instance- and viewpoint-equivariant. This ensures that descriptor values at corresponding world coordinates share identical features regardless of the object's instance or the camera's position and orientation. We evaluate our method using synthetic data and both 2D and 3D cameras on real-world data, confirming that the 3D equivariant nature of our approach facilitates generalization over 6-DoF poses and new object instances. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our technique achieves state-of-the-art results in repetition tasks using only 3D data. of object instances using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has garnered significant attention. Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter, CNNs regress intermediate features like 3D coordinates, semantic keypoints, or virtual control points in the first stage, with object pose subsequently determined through correspondence constraints derived from these cues. This paper focuses on refining the postprocessing stage of a two-stage pipeline by integrating projection grouping and correspondence learning to estimate poses in challenging scenarios. First, a local patch-based method predicts projection heatmaps representing the confidence distribution of 3D bounding box corners. A proposed projection grouping module then eliminates redundant local maxima across heatmap layers. Rather than directly applying the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithm to 2D-3D correspondences, multiple correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and their neighborhoods, then ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Finally, high-confidence correspondences are selected to determine the object's pose. Extensive experiments across three public datasets show that the proposed framework surpasses several state-of-the-art methods. Notably, by leveraging projection grouping, our framework significantly outperforms the baseline when up to 30% of feature heatmaps are occluded. Additionally, our approach exceeds the current accuracy record on the MPI Sintel correspondence evaluation set. The source code is available at https://github.com/MuZhengZheng/ProjectionGroupingPose.

This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. Similar to standard eigenvector centrality, a node's importance in a specific layer is derived from the weighted sum of its neighbors' importance within that same layer. However, unlike the standard approach, our framework allows the adjacency relationships and the importance values of neighboring nodes to originate from different layers. Crucially, this capability is only partially addressed by current multilayer eigenvector centrality frameworks, which typically rely on inter-layer edges to model such dependencies. In our proposed model, constrained, layer-specific eigenvector centrality scores are determined by a system comprising independent eigenvalue problems and dependent pseudo-eigenvalue problems, which can be solved efficiently through an interleaved power iteration algorithm. Additionally, we extend this work to allow constrained, layer-specific eigenvector centrality scores to depend on unconstrained, layer-specific scores from a potentially different layer, further generalizing the model with interleaved power iteration algorithm support. Finally, we present numerical results demonstrating that scaling issues often encountered when applying existing multilayer frameworks to compute such scored scores in practice can be resolved efficiently using our proposed approach. Although this paper focuses on directed graphs, the algorithm can also accommodate scenarios where layers consist of undirected graphs. By examining extensive families of four-dimensional Type IIB $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify potential generalized global symmetries and demonstrate how they are circumvented. A key component in these theories involves generalized $\theta$-terms, which establish non-linear interactions between axion fields and gauge field strength terms quadratic in topology, thereby disrupting a significant portion of global symmetries. Furthermore, assuming the presence of charged states can break any remaining residual symmetries. However, we show that generalized $\theta$-terms induce a generalized Witten effect, implying that the charged state spectrum forms an infinitely populated lattice. We also demonstrate that this lattice arises from the monodromy transformation acting on the moduli space boundary where the effective theory is defined. While we have illustrated how generalized $\theta$-terms create obstructions to global symmetries and how the resulting charged state spectrum violates any remaining generalized global symmetries, the latter mechanism appears to be a universal feature across various four-dimensional effective field theories.

Quantum acoustic cavities and resonators are instrumental in investigating these multi-phonon phenomena through both theoretical and experimental lenses. Specifically, this work examines a system comprising a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser and coupled to an acoustic cavity. While such systems exhibit fascinating multi-phonon behaviors, previous descriptions of the quantum dot were restricted to a two-level model, limiting the complexity inherent to real semiconductor quantum dots. In contrast, our proposed model incorporates both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot; the latter are especially valuable due to their reduced decoherence rates, as they do not undergo spontaneous photon emission. Within this framework, we demonstrate that by precisely adjusting the driving laser frequency, one can induce giant Rabi oscillations between the vacuum state and a dark exciton state involving $N$-phonon bundles. This approach highlights two significant achievements: first, it enables the creation of dark state excitations in the quantum dot without requiring the conventional external magnetic field; and second, in a dissipative environment where both the acoustic cavity and the quantum dot experience losses, the system functions as a "phonon gun," capable of emitting $N$-phonon bundles. Finally, our model aligns seamlessly with existing experimental setups, and we provide explicit numerical parameters based on Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) to facilitate future empirical investigations into this intriguing multi-phonon physics.

We hypothesized that this phenomenon significantly influences online misinformation dissemination because, despite their global potential, digital interactions are inherently localized, with interaction likelihood dropping sharply as distance increases. Analyzing over 8 million Reddit comments containing news links from January 2016 to December 2019, we discovered that Reddit does not function as a "hype machine" for misinformation as other platforms do; instead, it operates as a supply-and-demand system. Specifically, the volume of misinformation news scaled linearly with the population of each state (scaling exponent $\beta=1$, $R^2 = 0.95$). Moreover, variations from this universal trend were best predicted by state-level personality and cultural attributes ($R^2 = \{0.12, 0.39\}$), rather than socioeconomic factors ($R^2 = \{0.15, 0.29\}$) or political characteristics ($R^2 = \{0.06, 0.19\}$). We observed that states with residents exhibiting lower conscientiousness and cultures characterized by loose norms (low cultural tightness) experienced higher-than-expected circulation of all news categories, including fake news. Finally, in a temporal analysis, we found that the demand for misinformation did not escalate following the 2016 US presidential election, contrasting with patterns seen in Twitter and Google news trends. In summary, while the homogeneous sorting of Americans into geographic silos limits the local spread of misinformation, this demand is not driven by specific political factions but is intrins linked to certain cultural and personality traits of those who remain isolated from diverse viewpoints. These insights may help clarify why certain states become hotspots for specific types of misinformation.

Ionization fluctuations of nearby interface charges constitute a primary source of optical spectral diffusion for individual quantum emitters, a phenomenon that complicates their use as photonic quantum processors and sensors. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context. Finally, we introduce ContextNet, a simple module that explicitly enhances context usage in single-stage detectors by integrating selected featuremaps from distant regions. validated by our controlled dataset and a real-world scenario, ContextNet achieves an mAP gain of 2.6% over the baseline on MS COCO. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/haotianq/ContextNet. Object detection systems, whether single-stage or multi-stage, have limited receptive fields, causing them to struggle when foreground objects occupy only a small portion of the image. ContextASPP explicitly introduces global context into the model and is easily integrable into any existing single-stage detector. Named after its inspiration, the 'Eye' can focus on both local and global contexts simultaneously, unlike the 'Ear' of single-stage detectors, which has difficulty perceiving distant global information due to its limited receptive field. By adding ContextASPP to the RetinaNet family, we achieve an mAP gain of 3.0% on the MS COCO detection benchmark with negligible cost in terms of parameters and FLOPs. This leads to an empirical assessment of the model's ability to capture structures in a corpus of approximately 42 million financial news articles spanning 12 years. Utilizing the widely recognized Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists, we show that embeddings are prone to conflating terms with opposite polarity, as the model treats antonyms as frequentist synonyms. Additionally, we investigate the undocumented non-stationarity of this financial corpus through time series analysis of cosine similarities between groups of polarized words and company names, revealing that embeddings capture a complex mixture of English semantics and word distributions that is difficult to disentangle. Finally, we discuss the limitations of this approach for NLP applications. Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current algorithms necessitate an exponential number of samples relative to the player count to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper introduces the first family of efficient algorithms capable of learning rationalizable Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) with sample complexities that are polynomial in every problem parameter, including the number of players. To accomplish this, we also propose a new, efficient method for identifying a single rationalizable action profile (which need not be an equilibrium), significantly improving upon the sample complexity achieved by Wu et al. (2021). Our approach integrates several innovative techniques to ensure both rationalizability and no (swap-)regret, such as a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which may hold independent value. We further validate our findings with a sample complexity lower bound that demonstrates the tightness of our guarantees. Additionally, we provide an implementation of our algorithms alongside a set of synthetic and real-world experiments featuring a novel matrix game, illustrating how the sample complexity of learning CCE (and CE) generally exceeds that of learning Nash equilibria, with this gap widening as the action space expands. Our codebase is accessible at https://github.com/yashmehta19/RationalizableEquilibriaEfficientALG.

Equilibrium concepts serve as a cornerstone in analyzing strategic interactions; however, the sample complexity required to learn many is often prohibitive. This work offers an efficient algorithm for learning a rationalizable coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) within generalized sum games featuring exponential action spaces. By combining this with a previous finding of ours regarding the efficient learning of a single rationalizable action space, we achieve an sample complexity bound of ${\cal{O}}(T^{2/3})$, which is tighter than the ${\cal{O}}(T^{3/4})$ bound for general rationalizable action profiles. Our method builds a foundation on the "pessimistic" learning algorithm for correlated equilibria developed by Mehta et al. (2023). Experimental results on synthetic games and the "Big Match" demonstrate that the sample complexity for learning rationalizable CCE exceeds that for Nash equilibria, a discrepancy that intensifies as the size of the pure strategy space grows. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/yashmehta19/RationalizableEquilibria

The network structure follows an Erdős–Rényi random graph, but susceptible individuals adjacent to infectious nodes may sever or rewire these links during the epidemic. We derive large-population limits that establish convergence for the initial branching process phase and, under the assumption of a major outbreak, for the subsequent epidemic phase, which approaches a deterministic model equivalent to a specific pair approximation. Additionally, we obtain law of large numbers results for the final size of a major outbreak. Two key findings emerge across various parameter configurations: (i) the limiting proportion of infected individuals can exhibit a discontinuity at the critical infection rate $\lambda_c$, resulting in an abrupt jump from zero to a positive value, and (ii) when rewiring is restricted to uninfected individuals, this discontinuity causes the final infected fraction to leap from $0$ to $1$ as $\lambda$ crosses $\lambda_c$. Finally, we explore the interplay between these discontinuities and the conditions under which the final size follows the law of large numbers, particularly in the vicinity of the critical threshold $\lambda_c$. These theoretical insights were validated through extensive computer simulations. The described discontinuities in the final size represent a novel phenomenon within the context of SIR epidemics on networks.

While classical experience replay enables agents to retain knowledge by reusing past observations, its uniform sampling strategy treats all data points equally, neglecting their varying significance. To address this, we introduce a general Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER) framework that selectively prioritizes the most relevant samples to refine policy gradient estimates. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate that VRER accelerates the convergence to an optimal policy and boosts the performance of leading policy optimization methods. We introduce the MultiTalk Dataset, a collection exceeding 320,000 written dialogue sentences that achieves a balance between a high branching factor (10) and multiple conversation turns (6) via selective branch continuation. We offer several contributions aimed at advancing dialog generation within this highly branching context. To assess a diverse range of generated outputs, we propose a straightforward scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, designed to maximize the correlation between generated texts and human-referenced predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate successful applications of this scoring method both in a controlled setting for generating diverse outputs and within a real-world context for personalized recommendations. Experimental results show that our approach effectively captures a broad spectrum of generated dialogues, exhibiting a level of reference understanding comparable to a sentence-level baseline while simultaneously producing a more diverse set of responses. Conversational AI has seen significant development and public interest, yet most existing written dialogue datasets consist of fixed scripts. In contrast, we present a unique dataset featuring high branching factors and a moderate number of turns, facilitating the training and evaluation of dialogue generation across multiple dimensions. We conduct experiments on automatic dialogue generation and recommendation tasks, demonstrating improved performance in both areas.

Training large language models (LLMs) for natural language generation requires substantial computational resources and extensive human supervision. To address this, we introduce a new framework that leverages the semantic comprehensiveness of sentence-level references to encourage diverse and accurate text generation. Our method integrates the diversity of these references into a novel evaluation metric; unlike traditional metrics that penalize deviation from a single standard, our approach calculates a score representing the diversity of a set of generated sentences relative to a collection of sentence-level references. We apply this framework to various LLMs and dialogue generation scenarios, consistently observing performance improvements in both predictive accuracy and response diversity. Our code is open-source at https://github.com/divyansh12345/MultiTalk.

**Introduction**
Natural language generation has been extensively studied since the 1960s, with dialogue generation representing a core component of this field. While significant progress has been made in single-turn generation, multi-turn dialogue remains a challenging research area. Although the potential for diversity in single-turn generation is limited only by computational cost, maintaining a wide variety of interesting responses across multiple turns is significantly more difficult. The primary obstacle is the lack of appropriate evaluation metrics;

This work details the code's implementation, validates it through numerical tests, and presents initial findings from an extensive suite of cosmological simulations covering three categories of MG models featuring conformal coupling: $f(R)$ gravity, symmetron, and coupled quintessence. Built upon the parallel particle-mesh framework GLAM, MG-GLAM utilizes an efficient multigrid relaxation method to resolve the characteristic nonlinear partial differential equations inherent to these models. Specifically for $f(R)$ gravity, we have integrated novel variants to expand model diversity and optimized the relaxation algorithms to ensure sustained computational performance. While this paper focuses on conformal coupling, a companion study addresses derivative coupling MG models, such as Vainshtein and K-mouflage types. MG-GLAM serves as a versatile and broad platform capable of modeling prototypes for most significant MG theories. The code is highly optimized, achieving a speedup exceeding one hundred times that of previous $N$-body codes while maintaining high accuracy in predicting the matter power spectrum and dark matter halo abundance. Consequently, MG-GLAM is exceptionally well-suited for producing large volumes of MG simulations required for constructing mock galaxy catalogues and generating precise emulators for current and upcoming galaxy surveys. MG-GLAM is now available for download at http://www.lamost.org/mg-glam/. Since the code supports the simulation of diverse MG models with both vector and tensor degrees of freedom, it can significantly advance the observation, analysis, and interpretation of galaxy clustering and lensing in future surveys. We anticipate that MG-GLAM will be extensively utilized to conduct parameter inference from galaxy surveys, thereby tightening constraints on MG model parameters and enhancing our capacity to detect deviations from general relativity.

This accuracy allows for model-dependent inferences of MG parameters by comparing empirical data with waveform templates generated via numerical relativity or effective field theories. In this work, we construct GFF-valued processes on the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$ and the first orthant $\mathbb{O}$ by coupling a GFF with a time-evolving multiple SLE on each domain. We demonstrate that a GFF on $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{O}$ is locally coupled with a multiple SLE when the latter is driven by the Dyson model (a stochastic log-gas on $\mathbb{R}$) and the Bru–Wishart process (on $\mathbb{R}_+$), respectively. Consequently, we derive pairs of time-evolving domains and associated GFF-valued processes. Furthermore, by utilizing the reflection principle for the GFF, we show that imaginary surfaces can be constructed from single SLEs on the Riemann sphere equipped with the conformal welding measure, as well as from multiple SLEs on the real line with a corresponding cooling measure. This result generalizes a finding by Cheliotis regarding the reflection principle for time-evolving multiple SLEs on the Riemann sphere. Our main finding offers a converse to a result by Hamana and Shioya concerning the spatial MCW (multiplicative Cauchy transform) process on the orthant $\mathbb{O}$. Additionally, we provide a characterization of a pair of time-evolving domains derived from the Dyson model, confirming a result by Biane and Yor on the multiplicative Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}_+$. During these constructions, we also establish the existence of a measure we term the welding measure for SLE on the real line, which serves as a precursor to the GFF's conformal welding measure. These measures extend naturally to the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$. Our constructions of imaginary surfaces on $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{O}$ are rooted in previous research by the author on the reflection principle for the GFF and time-evolving multiple SLE. As an application, we revisit the correspondence between the Dyson model and the Hermitian Aggregation (HA) model on $\mathbb{R}$, a connection first observed by Sasamoto and Spohn

Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes indicate that reaction rate oscillations stem from Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings disturbing the jet flame. These findings align well with LES simulations regarding the mode shapes of both velocity and reaction rate fluctuations. Overall, this research highlights the efficacy of utilizing a linearized RANS-EBU model to capture the primary unstable mode in a reacting jet exposed to acoustic forcing, a result that correlates closely with LES-derived LES-derived velocity and reaction rate fluctuations. Introduction into combustion systems by external disturbances, such as acoustic fluctuations, can trigger Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings, which influence flame noise and noise-generated mode shapes. Capturing these phenomena necessitates high-fidelity LES or DNS simulations, which are computationally prohibitive for practical industrial applications. This paper linearizes a RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model to linearly analyze a methane-air jet flame subjected to acoustic actuation. The primary objective is to determine the mode shape of reaction rate oscillations arising from incoming velocity acoustic perturbations. , nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, when applying NLG to derive the rotation curves of spiral galaxies under the assumption of axisymmetry and steady-state conditions (where the constitutive relation remains applicable), the results indicate that these curves do not exhibit the previously reported excessive rise at intermediate radii [22]. Finally, the constitutive relations for both nonlocal electrodynamics and NLG are shown to maintain a close analogy. However, a key distinction exists: unlike in nonlocal electrodynamics, the constitutive relation in NLG lacks local limiting cases other than the local approximation. This limitation hinders the adoption of NLG as a theoretical model for galaxy dynamics. To conclude, the constituent material assumed to generate nonlocal effects in galaxy constitutive relations is briefly discussed. These findings rely on the adoption of the constitutive relation by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [22].

We present a statistical framework that leverages genome-wide association statistics to pinpoint classes of genomic elements that are either enriched for or depleted regarding loci influencing a specific trait, with the model inherently accommodating multiple annotation types. Applying this approach to GWAS data for 18 human traits—including red and platelet cell metrics, glucose and lipid levels, height, BMI, and Crohn's disease—we assessed the relevance of 450 genomic annotations across over a hundred tissues and cell lines, covering protein-coding genes, enhancers, and DNase-I hypersensitive sites. Our results indicate that the proportion of phenotype-associated SNPs affecting protein sequences varies by trait, ranging from approximately 2% for platelet volume to roughly 20% for LDL cholesterol. Additionally, we observed significant depletion of repressed chromatin for SNPs linked to several traits and enrichment of cell type-specific DNase-I hypersensitive sites for others (e.g., spleen-specific sites for platelet volume). Finally, re-weighting GWAS results using functional genomics data increased the count of high-confidence associated loci by approximately 5%. However, shifting from common to rare variants would likely exacerbate the challenge of integrating functional genomics data to predict which alleles drive complex traits.

Since the Human Genome Project, researchers have worked to link genetic variation to human disease and complex traits. Although GWAS have identified thousands of loci associated with common diseases and quantitative traits, the underlying causal variants and their mechanisms of action are known for only a few hundred. This study offers a statistical method to assess the functional relevance of genomic DNAs across diverse human traits, across different annotation types and biological contexts, and in light of the uncertainty inherent in GWAS. By integrating DNase-I hypersensitive site annotations from specific tissues, we recovered expected findings such as the high proportion of protein-altering SNPs among variants affecting platelet volume. Our analysis of 18 traits across hundreds of annotations reveals that DNase-I hypersensitive sites from a smaller set of cell types and tissues account for a larger share of associated variants, including enhancements for spleen and T-regulatory cells. Although using functional genomics to prioritize rare variants could yield more immediate scientific and clinical advances, the current state of DNase-I knowledge limits the potential to transform GWAS for genetic architecture analyses.

Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a hundred years for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that most likely remain undetected. We argue that dismissing these longer recurrence times based on dynamical modeling and the lack of millisecond pulsars in the appropriate mass range constitutes ad hoc constraints. Ultimately, we contend that the plausibility of a significant black hole population in the Galactic Centre relies on assuming that a primary fraction of neutron star LMXBs exceeds a century between outbursts—a premise that contradicts existing data. Consequently, we conclude that current information regarding variable sources in the inner few parsecs of the Galaxy offers no compelling evidence for the presence of stellar-mass black holes. Recent findings indicating that many variable sources in this region are likely cataclysmic variables further weaken the case for inferring black hole numbers in this environment.

Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The duration of these effects, which can persist for several picoseconds following excitation, depends on phonon decay rates. Enhancing these effects could establish a promising platform for manipulating localized quantum states or chemical reaction barriers through vibrational control. Furthermore, this phenomenon may have significant implications for the precision measurement of fundamental constants. Previously, our group demonstrated the existence of these phenomena using sum-frequency generation to probe zinc blende GaAs, validating the concept of several inertial phenomena in molecules and solids that can be engineered to manipulate chemical reaction landscapes or as fundamental constants. These include spin-rotation and centrifugal field coupling (analogous to the Coriolis effect), centrifugal spin-orbit and centrifugal relativistic mass coupling (analogous to the centrifugal effect), and centrifugal redshift (analogous to gravitational redshift). The magnitude of these effects can be increased by amplifying ion displacements. Our prior demonstration in GaAs provides direct evidence of these phenomena and suggests that terahertz forces may offer precise control over electronic quantum states or reaction barriers. Our previously established scaling laws indicate that these effects are even more pronounced in smaller molecules, such as those encountered in ultra-cold physics or chemical reactions. Finally, precise molecular oscillators, as demonstrated in this work and previously for specific molecules, can serve as highly sensitive probes for fundamental constant variations, potentially exceeding the sensitivity of current methods by nine to twelve orders of magnitude. Similar to the classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, this includes spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The magnitude of these effects can be enhanced and can directly influence chemical reaction barriers. This mechanism in small molecules offers a novel and powerful method for manipulating quantum states of interest or fundamental constants. Our previously established scaling laws indicate that these effects are even more pronounced in the ions of small molecules than in X-ray environments or thermal conditions, making them potentially relevant to various fields including ultra-cold atoms, chemistry, and materials science. First, we introduce a new metric leveraging Natural Language Inference (NLI) to assess the semantic variety of a model's response set. Validated against an existing framework (Tevet and Berant, 2021), our findings strongly suggest that NLI Diversity aligns with semantic diversity; notably, the contradiction relation proves more effective than the neutral relation for this purpose, and integrating the NLI model's confidence yields state-of-the-art performance. We employ the rapid rotation code Gyrorenter to simulate surface entropy profiles with various rotational velocities to assess how spin affects the minimum mass capable of sustaining stable hydrogen fusion. Our results indicate that even a modest spin of $\Omega/ \Omega_{\rm crit} = 0.05$ can raise the lowest-mass star able to burn hydrogen by $10^{-4}$ solar masses. Furthermore, we utilize the MESA stellar evolution code to simulate the full structural and thermal evolution of low-mass stars endowed with rapid surface rotation, derived from the rapid rotation framework. Our simulations cover a range of initial masses and rotation rates, with the model predictions validated against observational data on active, rotating solar-type stars. Specifically, we track the changes in both stellar structure and thermal history as the surface entropy profile evolves as a function of time. While the open question of interior rotation profiles impacts the outcome of these models, we explore multiple scenarios, including the most extreme case of core superrotation. By employing an inverse problem approach, we constrain the magnitude of this effect by comparing model predictions with observed near-surface convection zone depths. Finally, we determine the threshold central overpressure where relativistic effects cause the Chandrasekhar-Fermi limit to be exceeded, resulting in electron capture and halting further evolution. We also investigate the impact of rapid rotation on the mass of the degenerate core in binary systems and the emergence of oblate shapes in white dwarfs. Our findings align well with existing observations of rapidly rotating solar-type stars, the central overpressures in white dwarfs, and the Roche limit. Rapid surface rotation is found to shift the turning mass of white dwarfs approximately 0.15 $M_{\odot}$ across the investigated parameter space. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently calculating a data-driven Nash equilibrium restricted to the class of affine policies. Finally, we offer insights into the conditions necessary for the efficient computation of a Nash equilibrium. Although motivated by multi-agent search scenarios, these results have broader implications and may apply to other domains where direct best-response algorithms are absent. The proposed algorithm builds upon the generalized polymatrix transformation, a method previously introduced for task coordination in homogeneous multi-agent systems after natural conditions were met for its efficient execution. However, our work addresses the challenge of designing competing algorithms with disparate cost models under a diffuse cost distribution, a scenario where those prior conditions no longer hold. Best responses to general (non-affine) strategies remain computationally difficult; our algorithm is efficient provided the number of agents is polynomial relative to the square root of the dimension of the difficulty distribution's parameter space. Numerical experiments yield additional findings: (a) the algorithm is effective even when the actual dimension of the difficulty distribution is significantly lower than its maximum possible value, and (b) the square root scaling factor representing this difference is not strictly necessary, despite our algorithm's theoretical bounds relying on it. These experimental observations suggest that the performance of prior algorithms in such settings may also be analyzed using similar analysis techniques. To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. Consequently, reducing feature dimensions is essential for effective scaling. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. Additionally, PRFF offers superior scalability for both training and prediction in classification models, as well as efficient training and prediction for regression models, even on very large datasets. PRFF is readily implemented and significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art random feature techniques, as demonstrated in our experimental analysis. Furthermore, we provide comprehensive code, documentation, and examples available at https://github.com/hastie/PRFF. Experimental findings also suggest that tuning hyperparameters is unnecessary, as default settings yield optimal results.

Traditional methods for assessing attack effectiveness typically rely on macro-level metrics, like the critical percolation probability ($p_c$) and the size of the giant component, often overlooking the micro-level dynamics of node removals, their specific traits, and immediate outcomes. This paper introduces and applies a micro-scale approach to attack analysis. Grounded in network percolation theory, we examine the "avalanche" effect triggered by the removal of a single node from the giant component—a phenomenon where one removal causes a cascade of disconnections that significantly contributes to network fragmentation and immunization beyond the loss of that single node. We specifically analyze the avalanche size, defined as the count of nodes disconnected from the giant component due to one removal. Furthermore, regarding random attacks on Cayley tree networks, we analytically derive the distribution of avalanche sizes throughout the entire attack process, from initiation until the network is fully dismantled and the attack ceases. Our findings reveal a scale-free distribution indicating that avalanche sizes follow a power law across all stages of the attack, with an exponent of $\tau=2$. Additionally, we demonstrate that this power law exponent remains invariant regardless of the initial percolation probability. These results advance the understanding of the avalanche effect in Cayley tree networks and provide insights into the mechanisms of network immunization. The underlying mathematical framework, particularly the use of micro-scale analysis, can be extended to study avalanche phenomena in other contexts, including actual earthquake mechanics and black hole physics.

Additionally, we analyze the approach through a dialogue setting, offering insights into how the components contribute to performance. The core components of this approach were initially explored in a paper on machine translation (AMTA 2019), where additional experiments on a low-resource summary task were also conducted. An even earlier version of this work was presented at the Findings of NAACL 2019.

Machine translation has been a focal point of Natural Language Processing research for over five decades. Early methods, such as those by (Liang 1986) and (Philips 1991), relied on statistical language models to generate target words, selecting the word $y_i$ that maximized the probability $P(y_i|y_{<i})$. These models trained $N$-grams $N(y)$ from a development corpus and evaluated candidates using a linear combination of features, including a smoothed $N$-gram probability, a target-specific bias, and counts of overlapping substrings between the $N$-gram and the partial translation $y_{<i}$.

Our approach addresses these challenges by modeling occlusion and pose variations to decompose the complex task into several more tractable subproblems. 3D face reconstruction and alignment are fundamental yet difficult because of extensive pose and occlusion variations, which also make comprehensive evaluation challenging. In this regime, cosmological perturbations are amplified significantly, leading to a breakdown characterized by an enhanced scalar power spectrum and substantial negative values for the Bardeen potential. This deep sub-horizon environment proves conducive to primordial black hole (PBH) formation. Working in the spatially flat gauge with $\delta\phi\neq 0$, we explicitly demonstrate how perturbations in both the inflaton field and the background gravitational field drive these enhancements and subsequent PBH generation. We compute the parameters $\sigma(M)$, $\beta(M)$, and $f_\mathrm{PBH}(M)$ near peaks in the density contrast profile to estimate the current dark matter fraction attributable to PBHs across specific mass scales. Our analysis indicates PBH formation within the wavenumber range $0.43\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$ to $9.8\times 10^{13}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, corresponding to masses between $1.35\times 10^{-13}M_\odot$ and $2.60\times 10^{-16}M_\odot$. These objects exhibit evaporation times ranging from $7.74\times 10^{33}$ sec down to $5.53\times 10^{16}$ sec, and their present-day abundance varies from $0.016$ to $2500$. We plot $\log\left[ \frac{ \rho_\mathrm{DM}(z=0)}{\rho_\mathrm{PBH}(z=0)}\right]$ against mass to visually assess the potential for PBHs to account for all dark matter, and we also analyze the energy release from PBH evaporation and its impact on post-recombination CMB anisotropies. As this is the initial investigation into PBH formation via $\alpha$-attractors, the low-mass range identified here warrants more precise calculation and could be subjected to future observational tests. Keywords: PBH formation, $\alpha$-attractor models, CMB anisotropies, evaporation time, abundance.

Deutsch et al. to represent skew Dyck paths, these marked ordered trees serve as the subject of our study regarding the count of their deepest nodes. We derive explicit generating functions and determine that the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac{5}{3}$ as the tree size increases. This result contrasts with standard ordered trees, where the corresponding average approaches $2$. Additionally, we establish a combinatorial interpretation for this finding by demonstrating a bijection between marked ordered trees of size $n+1$ and pairs consisting of ordinary ordered trees of size $n$ and a node within them. The mean for marked ordered trees diverges from that of unified ordered trees, which is $11/5$ (reference { {CGLS20}}), because the marking of rightmost edges alters the proportion of trees featuring a unique deepest node. Furthermore, we provide a combinatorial argument showing that the difference between these two averages is exactly $1/5$. Along the way, various other combinatorial interpretations are also identified. Certain findings extend to a broader class of ordered trees known as $k$-skew ordered trees. Notably, a result by Banderier { {Ban06}} on conditioned random walks enables a straightforward determination of the limit for the average number of deepest nodes in uniformly random unified ordered trees, thereby reaffrasing a finding by Gouyou-Beauchamps { {Gou85}}. The proposed combinatorial structure intriguingly resembles the marked tournaments analyzed by Balier { {Bal12}}. Computer simulations supporting our main results are available on the authors' website. While previous research has examined over-parameterized linear models with non-sparse, high-dimensional data, those findings largely rely on the assumption of independent samples. This study investigates linear regression under over-parameterization with dependent time series data. We propose an interpolation-based estimator and establish a theoretical framework for its excess risk across various dependence structures. This approach accommodates infinite-dimensional data without requiring sparsity and unifies the handling of long-memory processes. Furthermore, we bound the risk using integrated covariance and the nondegeneracy of autocorrelation matrices. Our results indicate that convergence rates for short-memory processes match those of independent data, whereas long-memory processes decelerate convergence. Additionally, we provide examples of specific dependent processes applicable to this framework. Finally, simulation results demonstrate the validity of our findings, and the theoretical insights offer insights into the performance of similar estimators for highly dimensional time series data. **Keywords:** Over-parameterized linear regression, Time series, Long memory, Spline, Functional data, Nonasymptotic. **MathSubjClass:** Primary: 62M10; Secondary: 62G05, 62F12.

Introducing Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) offers a promising method for analyzing high-dimensional functional data. Although recent works have explored this avenue for functional time series, the process remains challenging due to core issues like dimensionality reduction, temporal dependency, and latent variable modeling. To address these challenges comprehensively, we develop a robust framework for analyzing dependent functional data through a novel VAE variant termed VAE-X. This model incorporates vector autoencoders, vector ARMA processes, vector latent variables, and specific independence conditions into a unified system. We provide complete theoretical support, including the existence and uniqueness of models up to finite dimensions, asymptotic behaviors of key components, and information loss metrics. Numerical simulations validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the model's capabilities. Additionally, we apply VAE-X to analyze COVID-10 data from 30 countries, offering insights into process dynamics and cross-country correlations. **MathSubjClass:** Primary: 62M04; Secondary: 62M10, 62H25, 62F12, 68U10.

izing low-carbon electricity grids. However, retrospective evaluations frequently highlight a concern that storage assets may not react adequately to intense price signals during scarcity events. Although this phenomenon is often blamed on forecasting inaccuracies or operational breakdowns, we argue it stems from risk-averse scheduling strategies. By applying a stochastic self-scheduling model to real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, we show that risk-averse storage units adopt a short-sighted operational approach. Specifically, they focus primarily on near-term price arbitrage, targeting only a limited number of extreme price peaks and valleys, which leaves them inactive during many periods characterized by significantly high or low prices. These findings carry significant policy weight, particularly given the lack of transparency surrounding unit-level risk aversion and the visible risks involved in intervention decisions. Consequently, regulators utilizing unit-based models for scarcity assessments may not fully grasp the actual capacity available to consumers. Our results underscore the necessity of adopting more unit-level aware approaches, such as pool-based optimization, for scarcity declaration assessments. In summary, this study is the initial attempt to empirically and quantitatively demonstrate that hoarding behavior arises from risk-averse storage units operating under stochastic dispatch models, and it highlights the potential for policy missteps when these units are managed with two-time-step lookahead periods in price arbitration.

The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction and dry convective adjustment schemes alongside a frictionless, non-divergent free-atmosphere regime governed by the rotating spherical Laplace-Taylor equations. Through linear stability analysis, a range of zonal symmetric Hadley cell circulation states is identified, evolving from symmetric to asymmetric (bifurcated) Hadley cells as the Coriolis parameter varies with latitude. Direct numerical simulations confirm these theoretical predictions in the GCM. While a single, zonal symmetric Hadley cell is typical for planetary-scale atmospheres, this study demonstrates that bifurcated (two-cell) circulation can emerge under specific conditions. The simulated two-cell circulations correspond to the previously documented "Stevens' circulations," characterized by an equatorial Hadley cell and a mid-latitude Ferrel cell separated by the subtropical jet. This mechanism underpins the divergence of Hadley cells in the model, offering a simplified representation of the physics necessary for such behavior in Earth-like atmospheres. Finally, a statistical analysis of how this two-cell circulation responds to solar insolation forcing, modeled as a latitude-wise cosine distribution, is presented. This response provides insights into the formation mechanism of Hadley cell bifurcation on Sun-like stars with Earth-like planets and how such bifurcations might shift under varying stellar luminosities. The findings reinforce the theoretical-predicted scaling law for the Hadley cell bifurcation point under solar insolation, which was originally established using the Shigeyama & Yoshida (SY) model. Notably, the simplified model successfully replicates the steeper slope of this scaling law observed in complex three-dimensional complex-neutral (CN) simulations. The simplified model also accurately represents the ratio between the rotation-period-dependent scaling factor and the SY scaling factor within CN simulations. These simplified model outcomes further congruent with those from a barotropic beta-plane model featuring friction and convection. Additionally, the study analyzes the similarities and differences regarding these scaling laws among the university models, SY simulations, and CN simulations by incorporating three-dimensional advection. AL designs are evaluated based on the predictive performance of the trained model relative to a baseline model constructed from uniformly sampled data. We investigate the space of AL algorithms characterized by three components: the scoring function, the verification method, and the optimization strategy. This framework encompasses popular AL methods, with support vector machines (SVMs) serving as a foundational example; linear AL algorithms are defined when the scoring function is linear. Our numerical results indicate that, for a fixed budget, AL performance scales with the square root of the sample size for both support vector classifiers and general linear scoring functions. Consequently, the performance gap between active and random learning narrows as sample size increases. Since evaluating the scoring function requires $O(n)$ time, we demonstrate that a pooled estimator can approximate the AL estimate with high precision using a minimal additional sample. Although this approach was previously suggested by Hotteling (1947), we provide detailed calculations of its statistical properties in the AL context. We validate these findings through simulations and a real-world example involving a credit card default dataset. Crucially, this method is particularly advantageous when the AL algorithm requires verification. Because the approach requires specifying only the sample budget, it functions as a plug-in solution that outperforms traditional AL methods in controlled tests. Current limitations include applicability to linear scoring functions and scenarios where the number of features $p$ satisfies $p \ll n$. Future work could extend this framework to high-dimensional settings ($p > n$) or develop adaptive sample size selection mechanisms. Additionally, while the approach was tested on support vector classification, other algorithms such as random forests, neural networks, and gradient boosting machines can also be incorporated. Although the current method requires the same computational cost as standard AL (linear in $n$), it offers significant advantages: it eliminates the need for iterative optimization, avoids potential local minima, scales efficiently to large datasets, and removes the risk of converging to suboptimal local solutions.

Our results indicate that $R_x(L)$ follows a universal scaling law, which can be effectively described by a diffusion model involving a competition between external and exchange interactions. Consequently, the combined problem of power allocation and scheduling becomes a mixed-integer non-convex challenge that is NP-hard. To address this, we introduce a low-complexity, decentralized framework that decouples power allocation from scheduling. In this approach, power is distributed centrally, while transmission modes are determined via a non-cooperative game aiming for a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. We evaluate two payoff calculation methods corresponding to different cross-interference power models and their associated communication overheads. Simulation results in a dense outdoor small-cell environment demonstrate that our proposed methods significantly outperform static TDD configurations. Furthermore, the outcomes indicate a clear performance-off trade-off between the power cross-interference models, suggesting the feasibility of adopting a more complex model to further enhance system performance. Notably, acceptable performance can be achieved even with minimal additional overhead compared to fixed TDD schemes. These findings are robust across various backhaul capacities and signal-to-noise ratio levels. The proposed method is directly applicable to current 4G networks for enhanced capacity and future 5G systems supporting device-to-device communications. Dynamic TDD, enabling independent uplink/downlink scheduling per cell, is essential for adapting to diverse and heterogeneous traffic patterns in small-cell networks. However, this setup risks inter-cell conflicts, making the optimization of cross-power allocation and transmission modes a critical research area for small-cell networks. Although the underlying problem is NP-hard, this paper proposes a decentralized solution where power is allocated centrally and transmission modes are scheduled through a non-cooperative game targeting a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. A key contribution is the derivation of a simple, distributed algorithm for time-mode allocation with low complexity, overcoming the challenges of stochastic power interference and discrete transmission modes that hinder traditional iterative water-filling methods. Two distinct payoff functions are investigated, revealing a clear trade-off between performance and overhead; simulations confirm substantial gains over static TDD even with low overhead, validating the use of a higher-interference cross-model. These findings are relevant for current LTE TDD enhancements and upcoming 5NRU designs. The core issues involve power allocation and transmission mode scheduling under potential inter-cell conflicts, forming a joint optimization problem that is NP-hard due to its infinite dimensions and discrete variables. While previous studies have explored related problems, this work uniquely focuses on time-division duplexing, employs a decentralized approach, and utilizes distinct payoff calculations. While BERT-based deep learning methods have yielded promising results, various approaches have been developed to incorporate structured knowledge for further enhancement. production in proton-nucleus collisions, utilizing proton-lead data from the CMS experiment at CERN's LHC, recorded at a nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 8.16$ TeV. The analysis focuses on events containing precisely one isolated electron or muon alongside a minimum of four jets, based on a dataset with an integrated luminosity of 174 inverse nanobarns. The observed $t\bar{t}$ signal exceeds the background-only hypothesis by more than five standard deviations. The resulting cross section of $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 45 \pm 8$ nb aligns with predictions derived from perturbative quantum chromodynamics. Furthermore, the data agree well with simulations from the POWHEG-MC@NLO and HERWIG 6 accounts. Beyond the significant implication of confirming top quark pair production in proton-nucleus interactions, this cross section carries important implications for dark matter research, as non-detected particles in the forward rapidity region within nucleus-nucleus collisions could indicate weakly interacting massive particles. This study represents a foundational step toward exploring beyond the Standard Model physics through proton-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we present the first measurement of top quark production in proton-nucleus events at the LHC, reporting a cross section of $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 45 \pm 8$ nb, which is 2.5 times larger than the corresponding value in muon-nucleus collisions. The reported cross section agrees with both POWHEG-MC@NLO and HERWIG 6 simulations and reflects approximately 1.2 times the cross section observed in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 8$ TeV. At the energy scale of top quark production, the strong interaction is moderately coupled, rendering this a rigorous test of perturbative QCD. Consequently, any discrepancies between data and theory could signal limitations in current QCD calculations or point to new physics, such as dark matter. We elucidate the reasons why comparing proton-nucleus and proton-proton data offers distinct advantages over other dark matter detection methods. This report serves as an introduction to a series of studies examining new physics via top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions, where the subsequent chapter delineates the characteristics of potential dark matter candidates accessible through this approach.

Formulating DP for graphs is challenging because data points are interconnected, often in non-linear or sparse ways, which complicates calculating individual privacy loss in differentially private learning. This difficulty is intensified by the lack of a single, established DP framework for graph settings, a problem that extends to GNNs and makes private machine learning on such data particularly difficult. Motivated by the absence of prior systematic research, we analyze graph-based learning from a privacy standpoint. We systematically review various DP formulations on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications within the GNN domain, and categorize existing work into graph analysis and graph learning tasks. These catalogues will feature high-resolution imaging and robust near-infrared spectroscopy, significantly influencing numerous fields of galaxy science. This review examines the potential scientific outcomes and prospects of Euclid across diverse domains, including the evolution of galaxies and active galactic nuclei (AGN), the local and early Universe, Milky Way and stellar population studies, supernovae and transients, Solar System objects, exoplanets, black hole demography, and galaxy groups and clusters. The development of galaxy clusters as standard candles has been significantly advanced by the Pantheon supernova sample, which demonstrates that the residual between the Millerband r-m (RMT) color and the rest-frame UV slope ($\beta$) maintains a consistent Hubble diagram from redshifts $z=0.06$ to $z=0.5$. By utilizing the full Euclid capability in detecting and characterizing galaxy clusters via XMM-Newton or similar instruments, we can refine these measurements and extend the accessible distance range. Specifically, we detail the feasibility of identifying $\sim 10^4$ clusters within each of the four Euclid deep fields, enabling the construction of galaxy cluster samples that serve as precise standard candles for cosmological inference. We outline the required cluster detection precision and the level of individual cluster characterization necessary to derive Hubble diagram residuals with a scatter of $\Delta\mu < 0.02$ (where $\mu$ is the magnitude per unit color) for clusters at $z<0.8$. These findings are directly relevant to the Euclid Working Group on Standard Candles and Clusters (EUGCC).

the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems. This work introduces a novel approach that yields stochastic trajectories of coherent hydrodynamic states, extending the methodology to encompass a broader range of quantum statistics. We demonstrate that the average state along these trajectories directly links to the quantum hydrodynamic path integral formulation, while the time-evolution operator is represented through a proper time discretization scheme. Consequently, the path integral expression for any observable acquire...Our findings advance the application of hydrodynamic methods to the dynamics of interacting quantum systems following abrupt changes, such as quantum quenches that alter Hamiltonian parameters or initial states. By utilizing this framework, we computed the dynamics of the interaction-to-temperature ratio within the one-dimensional Lieb-Liniger model, starting from various Bose-Einstein condensate initial conditions. Our results reveal that the evolution toward thermalization across diverse initial conditions can be accurately described by the Schrödinger-Heisenberg hydrodynamics of two fluid components, which emerge from the quantum pressure and residual quantum fluctuations of the dense gas. Moreover, the spatial profile of the interaction-to-temperature ratio exhibits oscillations during the evolution from the non-interacting regime, a phenomenon attributed to the interference of matter waves in the quantum gas. Finally, we propose using the in-situ density and rotation frequency (angular velocity) as observables for experimental implementations of this model on cold atom systems trapped in rotating harmonic potentials.

In the context of the annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of these words, the rate function corresponds to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of words. Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander \cite{BGdH10} established the quenched LDP (conditional on a typical letter sequence) for scenarios where renewal times exhibit an algebraic tail; their derived rate function consists of two components: the annealed rate function and a second term proportional to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of letters, where the reference law is generated by concatenating words and randomizing the origin. This proportionality constant matches the tail exponent of the renewal process. The current paper aims to generalize both LDPs to cases where the underlying letter sequences are not i.i.d. It demonstrates that both principles remain valid when the letter sequence satisfies a mixing condition known as \emph{summable variation}. The resulting rate functions are still expressed as specific relative entropies with respect to the reference laws of words and letters, respectively. However, because neither reference law is i.i.d., the extension requires several approximation arguments. A key component of this work is a decomposition of the Kullback--Leibler divergence for dependent processes, which may have independent applications. 64Ni nucleus has been significantly refined by integrating data from four experiments, which identified multiple 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV and determined their properties. The Monte Carlo shell model successfully reproduces these findings, revealing an unexpectedly intricate landscape of coexisting shapes. Notably, a prolate 0+ excitation was found at a surprisingly high energy of 3463 keV, with a collective 2+ state situated 286 keV above it; this marks the first such observation in Ni isotopes. Furthermore, the shift in the excitation energy of the prolate minimum across the neutron N = 40 subshell gap underscores the influence of the monopole interaction and its strength variations with N. These results are directly relevant to understanding the evolution of nuclear shapes and the location of shape phase transitions in the N = 40 region. The MCSD computations also indicate that 64Ni possesses three potential alpha-unbound states with distinct excitation energies and log ft values, implying that if the 64Ni(alpha, gamma) reaction proceeds via capture from the ground state, it would produce three isomeric 88Ni states with half-lives ranging from 0.3 to 10 seconds. Overall, this study offers insights into the formation and excitation energies of nuclear shapes, their impact on neutron capture cross sections, and the associated r-process conditions. However, because CV relies on random data partitioning, the resulting performance estimates are stochastic and can exhibit significant variability, particularly in natural language processing (NLP). We show that such unstable estimates are unsuitable for effective parameter tuning; consequently, the selected parameters are highly sensitive to data splits, often leading to sub-optimal choices and severe reproducibility challenges.

To address this, we propose employing J-K-fold CV, which utilizes J independent K-fold cross-validations to assess performance. Our primary contributions involve extending J-K-fold CV to the domain of parameter tuning and exploring strategies for selecting optimal values for J and K. We argue that minimizing variability is more critical than reducing bias for successful tuning, advocating for lower-than-typical values of K in NLP literature. This allows computational resources to be redirected toward increasing J. To validate the broad applicability of our recommendations, we examine a diverse set of case studies, including sentiment classification (both general and target-specific), part-of-speech tagging, and document classification. Our findings offer practical, evidence-based guidance for designing J-K-fold CV and selecting hyperparameters that is particularly relevant to researchers working with limited data.

Most probabilistic reasoning algorithms are specifically designed for particular types of probabilistic models. For instance, Variable Elimination (VE) [Rouhani1979] enables efficient inference in Bayesian Networks but struggles with Markov Networks, whereas Junction Tree algorithms [Henderson88] offer efficient inference for both, provided the network's separation width remains low. This paper proposes a unified, highly efficient algorithm for Bayesian and Markov Networks that supports core probabilistic inference, most probable explanation, and constrained optimization tasks. To achieve this integration, we develop innovative techniques for representing the most probable configurations of subsets of variables and compare them alongside existing methods in extensive numerical studies. Our results indicate that the algorithms we present are significantly more efficient than current state-of-the-art approaches for many commonly encountered probabilistic inference, most probable explanation, and constrained optimization problems. Alongside this research, we release a software library featuring implementations of these algorithms for various inference, most probable substructure, and constrained optimization issues across different graph-based probabilistic models. Source code and experimental datasets are available at https://github.com/NoamSharir/SHO-FAST.

a free-breathing, respiratory motion-compensated 4D (3D plus respiration) $T_2$-weighted turbo spin echo sequence suitable for radiology and MR-guided radiotherapy applications.

**Approach:** Continuous k-space data were collected using a rewound Cartesian acquisition with spiral profile ordering (rCASPR). This method was designed to match the contrast of conventional linear phase encoding while organizing data into multiple respiratory phases. Low-resolution, respiratory-correlated 4D images were reconstructed via compressed sensing to estimate non-rigid deformation vector fields, which facilitated motion-compensated image reconstruction. The rCASPR sampling technique was compared against linear and CASPR sampling regarding point-spread function (PSF) and image contrast through in silico, phantom, and in vivo studies. These comparisons utilized a linear 3D k-space parsing approach for T2-weighted image reconstruction. Finally, the rCASPR sampling method was evaluated against linear sampling based on several metrics, including visual inspection, a contrast-based score, and quantitative analysis of myelin tracts.

**Findings:** rCASPR sampling produced a sharper PSF (assessed both visually and quantitatively) and demonstrated superior image contrast, as confirmed by quantitative myelin tract analysis. Participants in a visual contrast assessment found motions up to 2.5 cm difficult to distinguish between free-breathing and reconstructed images.

**Conclusion:** rCASPR sampling offers a practical solution for obtaining high-quality, 3D plus respiration, motion-compensated $T_2$-weighted images, which are essential for radiology and MR-guided radiotherapy. These findings also suggest that rCASPR can effectively replace standard linear k-space sampling in any multi-dimensional (nD) sequence, even when nD compressed sensing reconstruction is employed.

Since its introduction in 2018, the outer outer helical configuration has been a prominent topic in plasma physics due to its ability to mitigate transport and entrapment of superthermal particles, which are common in the current outer regions of tokamaks and heliotrons. In this study, we employ five-dimensional self-consistent field theory to calculate the equilibrium of this configuration. Unlike previous studies, we model the wall as a conducting surface rather than a perfectly magnetized one, as the wall's finite resistivity significantly influences the core plasma. By analyzing the behavior of key parameters across various wall current levels, we determined the maximum sustainable external current. Furthermore, by examining the radial electric field profile, we identified the bifurcation of the inverse cascading flow. These findings suggest that both the magnitude of the reverse cascading flow and the threshold for its onset are strongly dependent on wall resistivity. Additionally, we observed that the maximum sustainable external current decreases as the ratio of poloidal to toroidal external fields increases. Finally, we evaluated the trade-off between reduced turbulent transport and the increased structural complexity of the magnetic field when employing external coils, concluding that the outer outer helical configuration is a viable option for reducing transport,

This process involves aligning a preoperative CT-derived organ model with an intraoperative surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video. The task is complex due to factors such as sparse and noisy real-time data, numerous unknowns regarding tissue properties, and the influence of adjacent structures like retracted ribs and the reduced abdominal cavity. We introduce a new level sets-based method for non-rigid surface-to-surface registration that effectively integrates a dense prior of liver self-similarities directly into the optimization objective. Originating in the 1970s through the work of Las Vergnas and Häggkvist, the investigation of graphs with the PMH-property integrates three fundamental graph concepts: matchings, Hamiltonicity, and edge-colourings. This study focuses on cubic graphs, aiming to characterize those where every perfect matching aligns with a specific colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. We demonstrate that this condition is equivalent to the graphs being even-2-factorable (E2F), meaning all their 2-factors consist exclusively of even cycles. While bipartite cubic graphs trivially satisfy the E2F property, our analysis is restricted to non-bipartite cubic graphs. Although the PMH-property provides a sufficient (though not necessary) condition for a cubic graph to be E2F, the primary objective of this work is to define an infinite family of non-bipartite, E2F cubic graphs parameterized by two variables, which we term "papillon graphs." We further determine the specific parameter values under which these papillon graphs exhibit the PMH-property or are merely E2F, and we prove that papillon graphs with distinct parameters are never isomorphic. Additionally, we analyze when papillon graphs fail to be even-bookable and when their 2-factorizations are not unique. Our findings indicate that, aside from a few trivial exceptions, papillon graphs are always E2F, and consequently, they are typically PMH. Throughout this characterization process, we constructed numerous cubic graphs that are E2F but not PMH, and we establish lower and upper bounds for the count of non-uniqueness 2-factorizations within this class. Throughout this characterization, we utilized an algorithm detailed in this paper to support our theoretical results. This algorithm, along with the associated dataset, is accessible via a GitHub repository and will publicly available at the following URL: https://even-2factorable-graphs.github.io/. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents preliminary definitions and results; Section 3 provides the characterization of papillon graphs by their E2F and PMH properties; Section 4 addresses the non-uniqueness of 2-factorizations and the even-bookability of papillon graphs; and Section 5 concludes the study.
