We track the dynamical evolution of Pop III compact object binaries as cosmic structures develop, calculating how field stars' dynamical friction drives these remnants into NSCs. Subsequent evolution inside the clusters is modeled through repeated three-body interactions. The merger rates and time-dependent merger kernel are derived by linking the time-evolving binary distribution function with the merger timescale. Our results indicate a current merger rate of $0.05\,yr^{-1}$ ($10^{-5}$ per second of star formation) for a typical scenario, occurring primarily between neutron star (NS)-black hole (BH) and NS-NS combinations. However, for a specific subset of massive BH-BH binaries, we identify a "delayed peak" in the merger rate spectrum occurring $1$--$10$ Gyr after the onset of Pop III formation. This peak arises because many binaries are initially ejected from forming clusters but subsequently recoil back in during violent gravitational collapse events. This mechanism establishes a distinctive signature for the post-peak merger rates of Pop III BH-BH binaries as clusters evolve. Furthermore, the detailed characteristics of this delayed peak can be resolved by incorporating the core collapse of globular clusters. These findings suggest that future high-resolution astrometric and microlensing observations of galaxy centers will either confirm or refute the existence of this phenomenon. Consequently, the evolutionary trajectory of Pop III binary remnants offers viable explanations for the observed "surprising lack of mergers" in both elliptical and giant giant galaxy clusters. This includes accounting for the absence of events from the most massive black holes, the preference for low redshifts, and the selection effect of the LIGO/Virgo detection volume. Merger remnants from these systems may currently reside in the cores of massive galaxies or follow parabolic trajectories around galactic centers. We propose that next-generation detectors, such as the Einstein Telescope and LIGO III, are required to trace the full evolutionary path of these remnants. This serves as an introduction to our companion paper, which details the computational code and observational evidence supporting our findings. By integrating previous studies on dynamical friction and our calculated merger rate history, we demonstrate that the observed redshift distribution of local NS-NS mergers can be accounted for by the "delayed peak" scenario, assuming a universal initial binary fraction. Initially, the study focuses on a single-user, single-relay configuration, addressing a joint power optimization problem at the source and relay under individual power constraints for both nodes, with the goal of maximizing the end-to-end secrecy rate through optimal power allocation across sub-carriers. Subsequently, the research expands to a more complex multi-user, multi-relay scenario. Utilizing a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) approximation for the end-to-end secrecy rate, an optimization problem is defined to jointly optimize power allocation at the base station, relay selection, sub-carrier assignment to users, and power loading at each relay node. The objective is to enhance overall system security while adhering to independent power budget limits at each transmitter and exclusive sub-carrier allocation constraints inherent to OFDMA. A joint optimization solution is derived using duality theory, where dual decomposition enables the application of convex optimization techniques to determine power loading at source and relay nodes. Additionally, the paper examines an optimization for relay power loading, relay selection, and sub-carrier assignment given a fixed base station power allocation. Finally, a sub-optimal scheme exploring joint power allocation across all transmitting nodes with fixed sub-carrier and relay assignments is analyzed. Simulation results are provided to validate the performance of the proposed schemes.

a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. To address this constraint and maximize the potential of LSTMs, this paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, we introduce the FDHT-LSTM, a model based on a fully decomposed hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) structure that maintains high accuracy with ultra-low complexity. To leverage these algorithmic advantages, we designed a specialized hardware architecture capable of executing the FDHT-LSTM efficiently. Through a refined memory access scheme, the hardware supports complex matrix transformations in real-time without access conflicts. Evaluation results demonstrate that both the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator deliver superior performance. Compared to state-of-the-art compressed LSTMs, FDHT-LSTM offers order-of-magnitude reductions in model size alongside significant accuracy gains across various video recognition datasets. Furthermore, against the state-of-the-art tensor decomposed hardware accelerator TIE, our FDHT-LSTM architecture achieves higher throughput, better area efficiency, and improved energy efficiency on the LSTM-Youtube workload. Similarly, on the LSTM-UCF workload, our design outperforms TIE in throughput and energy efficiency while maintaining comparable area efficiency. To validate the effectiveness of our co-design approach, we conducted extensive experiments comparing different algorithmic and hardware configurations. These results confirm that our method optimizes the trade-off between accuracy, throughput, and energy efficiency. Source code for our framework is available at: https://github.com/zhengjiajun96/FDHT-LSTM.

We introduce a related yet distinct proposal: the conjecture should instead apply to particles possessing non-negative self-binding energy. This perspective is especially significant in anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, as it admits a straightforward conformal field theory (CFT) dual. Specifically, if $\Delta(q)$ represents the scaling dimension of the lowest-dimension operator carrying charge $q$ under a global $U(1)$ symmetry, then $\Delta(q)$ must be a convex function of $q$. Unlike formulations relying on holographic dual forces or spacetime locality, this approach allows us to boldly conjecture that charge spectrum convexity applies to any unitary CFT, extending beyond those with weakly coupled and weakly curved gravitational duals. We term this the Charge Convexity Conjecture and note its generalization to larger global symmetry groups. Testing this via perturbation theory, $1/N$ expansions, and semi-classical methods in examples where anomalous dimensions are calculable confirms the conjecture in all cases examined. However, the underlying CFT reason for this validity remains unclear. Furthermore, unlike the case for vacuum vacuum degeneracy, we cannot currently derive this charge convexity result from the nuclearity condition, a property known to hold for all CFTs. As a potential pathway forward, we speculate that a suitable generalization of the modular hamiltonian may offer the necessary perspective. Additionally, this framework could potentially extend to supersymmetric theories, where BPS state properties might enforce the necessary convexity, and to quantum gravity in AdS$_3$, where such a mechanism could explain the cardinality of the CFT bootstrap function. Although formulated for AdS$_3$, the underlying logic is expected to generalize to AdS$_{d\ge 3}$, implying that the $\mathcal{F}_p$ functions in the bootstrap are convex for $p>1$, a result already established by Polchinski and Saxc. Finally, we connect this work to recent findings on the convexity of operator dimensions with respect to quantum numbers in 4D $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory.

This study constrains the formation and dissipation timescales for vortices in both hemispheres, focusing on the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), characterized by higher temperatures and increased hydrocarbon levels at millibar pressures. While the NPSV began forming in late northern spring, it lacked the distinct thermal and compositional contrasts observed at the south pole during its southern summer by the end of Cassini's observations, shortly after the northern summer solstice. The new South Polar Stratospheric Vortex (SPSV) manifested with greater clarity: its thermal and chemical signatures were fully established within 21 $\pm$ 9 days of the southern summer solstice and returned to near-ambient temperatures and abundances 2.5 months later during southern autumn. During southern summer, the SPSV surface hovered just below the pole; as southern autumn progressed, it expanded, causing polar temperatures to rise above the passive infrared radiative equilibrium threshold, thereby triggering a secondary atmospheric heating source via longwave radiation absorbed by hydrocarbons. Consequently, the SPSV surface migrated poleward at roughly 1 km day$^{-1}$ (or 0.3 km day$^{-1}$ relative to the rotation frame) during the final four months of southern summer and the initial half of southern autumn, prior to the vortices' dissolution. During southern summer, the SPSV drove two distinct secondary heating events at pressures between 1 and 0.1 mbar, whereas the NPSV produced only a single, less intense event at ~1 mbar. Both hemispheres exhibited a delayed response to the solstice, with the SPSV taking about 21 days to fully establish and the NPSV requiring nearly 2 months. Both vortices also induced secondary heating events at high pressures (~5 mbar) that preceded the surface events by 3 to 4 months. Although the precise origin of the high-pressure event remains uncertain, it likely did not result directly from the vortex formation. After the high-pressure event, the temperature profile along isobars shifted from a source-dominated curve to one influenced more by the sink, indicating that the vortices had already begun to weaken before their surface events commenced. We demonstrate that solutions possessing negative energy exhibit finite-time blow-up. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is energy-subcritical and given further symmetry constraints, we establish blow-up governed by the same optimal ground-state criterion found in Holmer and Roudenko's work on $\R^{d}$. The traditional Glassey proof, which relies on the concavity of variance, is inapplicable in the presence of an obstacle due to boundary terms arising in the second derivative of the variance that carry an unfavorable sign. To address this, our primary approach involves introducing a novel modified variance that is bounded from below and strictly concave for the specific solutions under consideration. Further contributing to the challenge of directly handling boundary terms, our analysis on local well-posedness and blow-up requires precise determination of the domain of validity for the Poincaré and Sobolev inequalities, as these bounds depend explicitly on the solution and shrink as it approaches blow-up time. Accurately tracking these sharp constants is essential not only to maintain control over the solution but also to ensure the applicability of key analytical tools. To achieve this, we carefully analyze how both the Poincaré and Sobolev constants behave as the domain narrows, utilizing optimal Fourier-based estimates for the Poincaré constant and classical covering arguments for the Sobolev constant. Since its formulation by Colmez and Robba, the local monodromy theorem serves as a cornerstone in the local theory of $p$-adic differential equations, enabling the reduction of the irreducibility of 2-dimensional irreducible representations of local fields under a non-rigidity condition on the representation's monodromy. This concept was recently generalized to abstract algebraic groups by J.-F. Castella. In this paper, we present a non-standard proof of this extension and further generalize the result to a broader class of algebraic structures known as Hilbert rings. This class includes the ring of functions defined on any irreducible algebraic set, as well as the intersection of the rings of Hilbert polynomials for all families of ideals within a fixed dimension. The primary technical challenge in our approach lies in establishing a local monodromy theorem for the more abstract notion of non-rigidity regarding the Hilbert polynomial of a family of ideals, which necessitates a non-standard proof of the irreducibility of certain families of linear operators acting on powers of vector spaces. An auxiliary finding characterizing the non-degeneracy of specific irreducible representations of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over fields of positive characteristic is also included, as it may have independent significance. Additionally, the lemma proving the local monodromy theorem for the irreducibility of algebraic sets is of independent interest.

By leveraging the well-established theory of elliptic curves, we provide a complete characterization of the image of the local Langlands correspondence for this class. Specifically, for a fixed generic $\ell$-adic representation of the absolute Galois group of a non-archimedean local field, we determine all moduli of isomorphism classes of elliptic curves possessing that underlying representation. Furthermore, utilizing results by Clozel and Henniart, we establish the uniqueness of the associated L-function's coefficients modulo a specific ideal in the ring of integers of an elliptic function field over a quadratic extension of $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$, given a sufficiently precise knowledge of the representation. Consequently, we derive a novel, purely Galois-theoretic description of the isomorphism classes of elliptic curves over the maximal unramified extension of the ground field. This approach yields a new, non-classical method for constructing Hilbert Class Fields, distinct from traditional methods based on the inverse theorem for the Cr\^epeau-Ihara theorem. We also discuss connections to work by Coates and Greenberg, as well as findings by Merel regarding the images of global L-functions at integer points. Finally, we address the scenario where the local L-function vanishes at zero. The results presented here extend to a broad class of abelian extensions of local fields that contain a quadratic unramified extension.

The model represents fractures as $(d-1)$-dimensional interfaces within a $d$-dimensional domain, where $d$ equals 2 or 3. Fractures are categorized into two types based on the permeability contrast between the fracture and the surrounding matrix: those with significantly higher permeability are termed {\it conductive}, while those with significantly lower permeability are termed {\it blocking}. Conductive fractures are modeled using a standard hybrid-dimensional interface approach assuming continuous pressure across the interface, whereas blocking fractures utilize a recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach that enforces continuity of the normal Darcy velocity component. Additionally, the numerical method yields locally conservative velocity approximations and generates a symmetric positive definite linear system defined solely on pressure degrees of freedom located at the mesh skeleton. Benchmark tests in both two and three dimensions demonstrate the method's performance, with results showing it to be highly competitive against existing literature approaches.

Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific model assumptions and sample characteristics, such as composition and size. Furthermore, there is a lack of guidance on how these factors influence decisions across varying sample sizes. This study examines the behavior of Bayes factors in a simple statistical setting, explicitly accounting for dependent and missing data patterns—common issues in real-world scenarios that have yet to be thoroughly investigated in relation to Bayes factors. The findings reveal significant fluctuations in Bayes factors driven by both sample size and missing data mechanisms, ultimately impacting the chosen hypothesis. These results hold practical relevance, as many advanced statistical methods fail to address one or both of these issues. Consequently, there is an urgent need for updated procedures to adapt to contemporary data types and collection methods. To achieve this, new methodologies must be developed that remain robust and reliable, particularly when dealing with missing data. Although this paper focuses on Bayes factors, the proposed techniques are broadly applicable and can enhance the accuracy of various statistical methods, such as classification algorithms. The proposed distribution-free technique requires no parameters, is straightforward to implement, and functions effectively with both complete and missing data. Simulation studies and a real data example confirm the method's robustness, reliability, and efficiency, especially sample size-dependent, while also validating its practical utility. Although this approach was designed for parametric model fitting, its applications extend beyond this scope. Furthermore, the implementation code is accessible at http://www.siamhoseini.net/HBayesFactor to assist researchers in applying it across diverse fields. In summary, this paper introduces a distribution-free method characterized by its simplicity, accuracy, and broad applicability.

By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a Euclidean metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. These findings offer a complete geometric rationale for the enhanced performance of vanilla gradient descent in this context. Furthermore, under a weaker restricted strict convexity assumption, we establish that geodesic convexity holds in a neighborhood of local minimizers. Building on the proven effectiveness of activation clipping, this study constructs a preliminary safety case for classifier CNNs by showing that range supervision acts as a highly dependable fault detector and mitigator for relevant bit flips, specifically within an eight-exponent floating-point format. Deep learning is increasingly central to safety-critical vision systems, yet the industry often relies on heuristic architectures and training processes that lack theoretical grounding. This work proposes a theoretical framework for designing safety-critical, low-footprint classifier CNNs tailored to embedded devices with limited resources. The approach utilizes a patch-based, fully convolutional architecture where layers consist of carefully selected, safety-oriented hyperparameters. We present an automated search algorithm that selects a "default" ResNet-50 variant capable of classifying images of pedestrians, vehicles, and cyclists across three European cities with high accuracy. The resulting model is lightweight, requiring only 12 MB of memory and 22 MFLOPS of computation. An accompanying R package, `theoretical-safety-cnn`, offers classes for training, evaluation, and inference, including support for various multi-GPU evaluation strategies. The paper details the algorithm, provides empirical evidence of its theoretical and practical advantages over heuristic methods, and showcases the package through examples using the CityPersons and Cityscapes datasets.

Abstract title: Multilingual Embeddings via Common Semantic Spaces through Instance and Cluster Consistency.

Recent advances in monolingual word embedding models have enhanced natural language processing (NLP) for specific languages. However, deriving related representations across languages remains challenging in a sparsely supervised setting. Although recent multilingual embedding methods align individual words, this approach often lacks linguistic generality. This paper introduces a novel approach by aligning clusters of words instead. We define two types of clusters—morphological and semantic—and achieve cross-lingual consistency for both in a common semantic space. Our experiments across multiple NLP tasks, including language-agnostic name tagging and coreference resolution, show significant improvements, with an average F-score gain of $7.5\%$ for name tagging and an absolute gain of $3.5\%$ for coreference. Additionally, we release a new multilingual embedding model that exhibits increased similarity between linguistically related words compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Source code is accessible at https://github.com/coref-berkeley/ML-CCE.

Relativistic heavy-ion collisions serve as the primary experimental framework for probing the properties of matter at extreme energy and density conditions. A central objective of this research field is the creation and characterization of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP). Evidence for QGP formation includes the conversion of initial spatial eccentricity into collective flow, the suppression of particles with high mass-to-charge ratios, and a decrease in the proton-to-pion ratio relative to thermal expectations. Additionally, the enhancement of charmonium state suppression and the reduction of $\Delta$ resonance yields upon increasing collision energy indicate that high-multiplicity Xe-Xe collisions at the LHC are capable of reaching LHC-level densities. Understanding the connection between these phenomena and the emerging properties of the produced medium is essential for advancing nuclear physics knowledge. Although the LHC has significantly expanded the dataset of heavy-ion collisions, a direct comparison of the QGP characteristics found in lead-lead (Pb-Pb) collisions with those in xenon-xenon (Xe-Xe) collisions remains necessary.

9, Chile, particularly its capital Santiago, experienced extensive violence that resulted in the destruction of both public and private infrastructure. This study seeks to extend an epidemiological non-local model, previously effective in describing the 2005 French riots, to include the topological structure of Santiago's subway network and account for the observed spatial distribution of rioting. While the model accurately replicated the aggregated temporal progression of the disorders, it failed to reproduce the actual spatial pattern of activity in Santiago. This discrepancy is primarily due to the model's absence of a population displacement mechanism, a factor deemed essential for explaining the unrest episodes in the city. These findings offer insights into the underlying dynamics driving such events and highlight the critical role of key attributes, such as mobility, in constructing representative mathematical frameworks. Furthermore, the results suggest that applying the "law of power law" can provide additional predictive capabilities regarding the duration of these episodes. While directly observing all parameters governing this mechanism in real-time during future riots may be challenging, such data could potentially be estimated from initial signs of unrest, thereby enabling more accurate and precise forecasts. Ultimately, applying this approach during similar events could support authorities in making informed decisions regarding the allocation of human and material resources required to manage the situation effectively. Although this research concentrates on the specific context of riots in Santiago, it employs a general mathematical framework, suggesting its potential applicability to other locations with distinct urban layouts. However, before the model can be used for predictive purposes in new cities, its parameter values must be carefully calibrated to ensure they fully and accurately represent the specific characteristics of those environments.

. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days and water-covered terrain—scenarios where traditional VIO algorithms fail to extract visual features. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional and existing learning-based VIO baselines across various scenes. Additionally, comparisons with previous work highlight the model's efficiency in terms of both computation time and memory usage. Furthermore, since inertial memory is cleared every three seconds, this technique is particularly well-suited for robotics applications relying on Hand-Eye Integration (HEI) systems. We believe this technique will prove highly valuable in HEI-based service and agricultural robots. Incremental learning-based visual-inertial odometry (ML-VIO) offers a promising solution for estimating camera poses in specific场景, yet it remains vulnerable to drift during long-term operations, particularly when visual features change. To address this, we integrated complementary deep feature extraction with traditional Kalman filtering to precisely initialize the system upon entering a new scene. Furthermore, we developed a adaptive re-initialization strategy to reset the system when a familiar scene re-occurs, ensuring stable long-term localization. Experimental results indicate that this method enhances the system's adaptability to environmental shifts while maintaining high localization accuracy. Overall, our contributions improve initialization and re-initialization processes, resulting in a more robust long-term localization capability. In terms of visual features, both traditional and learning-based methods yield comparable results, whereas our approach significantly outperforms baselines when features are obscured. Compared to conventional filters, our technique reduces computational cost by approximately 50%. By combining the advantages of complementary space, Kalman filtering, and attention mechanisms, our method achieves superior performance. We present a comparative analysis of short-, medium-, and long-term experiments, confirming the stability and efficiency of our proposed approach. This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by adapting characteristics from its parent Hamiltonians. Our findings reveal that SHOWS supports both "Fermi-arc" surface states and hinge states linking the projections of Weyl points. We successfully constructed this exotic SHOWS state theoretically and observed it experimentally in three-dimensional (3D) stacked electric circuits featuring honeycomb-kagome hybridizations and double-helix interlayer couplings. These results pave the way for achieving square-root topology within 3D solid-state systems. SHOWS expands the diversity of square-root Hamiltonians beyond 2D, particularly within square-lattice 2D systems, by drawing inspiration from exotic 3D Weyl semimetal states, thus establishing a novel theoretical framework for exploring square-root topology lower than previously recorded 2D limits. Our results demonstrate that leveraging the full range of exotic topology can facilitate the realization of novel square-root phenomena. Specifically, we show how a SHOWS can generate honeycomb-like surface states with a work function and how hinge states can emerge from the projection of Weyl points. Furthermore, by utilizing the chiral anomaly induced by an external field along these hinges, we illustrate how a SHOWS can trigger hexagonal antiferromagnetic ordering via the Fermi-arc surface states. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of chiral-induced hexagonal antiferromagnetism arising from Fermi arcs within a SHOWS. We hope our work encourages further investigations into the fascinating physics of square-root higher-order topological materials.

These teachers possess pre-training tasks and datasets that are distinct and mutually unknown. Our motivation arises from a current challenge in model sharing: despite significant investments in training large, capable networks, researchers and institutions often cannot share their pre-trained models due to privacy, security, or intellectual property concerns, even when they wish to contribute. To better understand the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems, we investigate whether the QNEC constrains irreversible entropy production during quenches driven by energy-momentum inflow from an infinite memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories. Our findings indicate that while the increase in both entropy and temperature—mandated by the Clausius inequality of classical thermodynamics—is necessary to avoid violating the QNEC in quenches involving transitions between thermal states with momentum (dual to BTZ geometries), it is not sufficient. For any arbitrary initial state, we establish lower and upper bounds on the increase of entropy (or temperature) given a fixed increase in temperature (or entropy). These results provide concrete examples of quantum lower and upper bounds on irreversible entropy production, confirming their existence as previously theorized. Additionally, we observe a monotonic behavior in the non-saturation of the QNEC over time following a quench and analytically derive their asymptotic values. Our study demonstrates that the entanglement entropy of an interval of length $l$ consistently thermalizes within time $l/2$ with an exponent of $3/2$. Furthermore, we analytically determine the coefficient of the initial quadratic growth of entanglement for any $l$ and show that the slope of the linear growth of entropy after the "scrambling time" ($l/2$) increases as the initial slope of the curve decreases. Analytic results for small and large $\beta_0$ (or $T_0$) align with our numerical findings, and these numerical findings agree with previous results regarding the coexistence of quantum lower and upper bounds on irreversible entropy production after quenches. Ultimately, the QNEC serves as a robust tool for understanding the thermalization dynamics of local operators after quenches and demonstrates that two-dimensional quantum field theories adhere to the laws of classical thermodynamics on average. Our analyses reveal that the four semi-classical gravitational effects—Newton's law of cooling, the increase of entropy in isolated systems, the arrow of time, and the inequality of temperature—arise strictly from the quantum lower bound on irreversible entropy production, which corresponds to the quantum correction to the entropy of a thermal state. Finally, we analytically prove the existence of a quantum higher bound on irreversible entropy production for small spatial intervals. The processes that formed and evolved Venus's atmosphere to its current surface conditions remain subjects of intense debate, encompassing questions that span multiple disciplines. We investigate these interconnected mechanisms, beginning with volatile sources and sinks, and trace the path from the deep interior to the upper atmosphere, covering volcanic outgassing, surface-atmosphere interactions, and atmospheric escape. Additionally, we address complex historical factors, such as the impact of Late Accretion events, the connection between magnetic field generation and long-term evolution, and the effects of geochemical and geodynamical feedback cycles on the atmosphere. Based on modeling and observations, we outline plausible evolutionary pathways for Venus from accretion to its present state. Three specific scenarios are highlighted: first, desiccation caused by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase; second, a prolonged period of surface liquid water followed by climate destabilization and a runaway greenhouse effect; and third, inefficient outgassing that retained water within the planet, trapping hydrogen in the core and oxidizing the mantle. Finally, we discuss current evidence and the future observations and missions needed to refine our understanding of Venus's history and the intricate feedback cycles operating among its interior, surface, and atmosphere across past, present, and future timescales.

Among these, the Hawkes process is particularly popular due to its ability to define the probability of new events based on the process's history. This study focuses on the nonlinear Hawkes process, which effectively captures excitation and inhibition dynamics between different dimensions. Within a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we derive concentration rates for the posterior distribution regarding the parameters, assuming only mild conditions on the prior and the model. These findings also establish convergence rates for Bayesian estimators. Additionally, a key aspect of event-data modeling is reconstructing the interaction graph, or Granger connectivity graph. We demonstrate consistency guarantees for Bayesian approaches in estimating this structure, specifically proving that the Variational Message System (VIMS) method yields a consistent estimator of the Hawkes process parameters. Consequently, consequent procedures, such as testing the independence of streams and identifying inhibitive links, are also shown to be consistent. Bayesian consistency serves as a foundational element in guaranteeing the consistency of these derived estimators. Our main results include both theoretical and simulation-based evidence. To support these findings, we develop theoretical tools for assessing Hawkes process parameters and interaction matrices, particularly concerning their distance metrics. Furthermore, we establish theoretical bounds on the error of Bayesian estimators for these parameters and the interaction matrix, specifically for the Hawkes process under a VIMS posterior distribution. Finally, our empirical results confirm these theoretical bounds through simulations and an analysis of Twitter data regarding Earthquakes, Cell tower traffic, and Neurons. Our contributions are organized as follows: first, we introduce the modeling of multivariate point processes and the specific dynamics of the Hawkes process; subsequently, we present the Bayesian consistent modeling of this process; and finally, we outline the steps for the theoretical and empirical analysis of multivariate point processes, particularly the Hawkes process. The empirical section comprises four subsets of experiments designed to validate our theoretical findings. We conclude with a discussion of our results and potential directions for future work. Alongside the theoretical and empirical sections, an auxiliary section provides proofs for our theoretical assertions, accompanied by lemmas and auxiliary lemmas that support these proofs. Additionally, there is a dedicated section containing auxiliary lemmas and experiments regarding the theoretical analysis of the interaction matrix. The supplementary material offers further details on the empirical analysis, and a separate section lists the required packages for reproducing the paper's results.

Identified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a notably brief plateau phase ($67.0 \pm 0.6$ days), SN~2020jfo displays a fainter peak absolute $V$-band magnitude ($M_V = -16.90 \pm 0.34$ mag) compared to other Type II SNe with similar or shorter plateau durations. By analyzing the relative intensities of [Ni~II] $\lambda$7378 and [Fe~II] $\lambda$7155, we determined a Ni/Fe production ratio of 0.08, roughly 1.3 times the solar abundance. Spectral modeling of the nebular phase, alongside semi-analytical approaches, indicates that this elevated ratio stems from an excess of $^{60}$Ni (which decays into the isotope Ni-58) relative to other nickel isotopes. Given that Fe-60 and Ni-60 are predominantly generated via neutron capture during the late stages of stellar evolution, this implies a pre-main sequence history characterized by extensive deep convective zones and extensive mass accretion. SN~2020jfo thus represents the second least luminous Type II-SNe with a prolonged plateau phase that exhibits such prominent [Ni~II] emission, serving as a compelling case study for investigating the progenitor systems of Type II supernovae and the neutron capture processes within them. In this MuLE setup, a single LE mirror is partitioned into multiple segments, directing X-rays reflected from each segment to distinct quadrants of one or more detectors positioned behind the mirror. Designed with quasi-static evolutionary applications in mind, our method utilizes a custom-developed Lagrangian formulation. Unlike the standard Eulerian approach, this formulation solves force balance equations to determine the positions of fluid elements mapped to grid points. Distinct from prior literature, we do not rely on the first integral of the Euler equation, which typically lacks a general analytic solution. Instead of prescribing the spatial distribution of angular velocity or angular momentum as previous methods do, we assign specific mass, angular momentum, and entropy to each fluid element; the angular velocity and momentum distributions are subsequently derived once the positions of all elements are established. We discretize the time-independent Euler and Einstein equations using the finite-element method, resulting in a large system of nonlinear algebraic equations that we solve via our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. To validate this formulation, we have constructed both barotropic and baroclinic rotational configurations and solved three evolutionary sequences that simulate cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion as simplified toy models. By successfully implementing a relatively complex physical process, our formulation demonstrates significant potential for investigating star and binary compact object evolution. This new Lagrangian method offers distinct advantages over the conventional Eulerian formulation, and we anticipate that algorithmic improvements will further enhance its capability to model binary star evolution. Finally, we emphasize that our state-of-the-art algorithm represents a state-of-the-art achievement in the field of binary compact object research.

For events involving neutron stars, the concurrent detection of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation offers significant potential to deepen our understanding of these phenomena and investigate the equation of state of dense matter. This study introduces the first deep learning-based classification model for GW signals arising from NSBH mergers, utilizing the time-frequency representation of GW data. This proposed roadmap commences with the immediate need to develop a similar learning model capable of identifying GW signals from BBH and NSBH in real-time LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA data. We conclude by highlighting the analytical techniques and computational strategies employed in this analysis, which are applicable to every step of this future roadmap. This study examines shifts in the income diversity of urban interactions across various pandemic phases, leveraging a privacy-preserving dataset of over one million anonymized mobile phone users from four major U.S. cities, spanning three years before and during the crisis. Urban interactions and encounters are vital for stimulating innovation, enhancing community resilience, and fostering diverse populations. Despite their significance, there is a lack of empirical evidence regarding how specific pandemic policies influence the diversity of encounters in mid-sized cities, particularly as societies consider easing restrictions in late 2021 and beyond. This paper analyzes changes in encounter diversity before, during, and after the pandemic in five mid-sized U.S. cities, and tracks the trajectory of diversity metrics over one year post-pandemic onset. We find that epidemics can cause sustained reductions in the diversity of urban interactions, with urbanites in mid-sized cities reducing their willingness to meet individuals from novel income backgrounds by up to 25% more than a year after the pandemic began. These findings are derived from high-volume mobile phone data on individual trajectories, aggregated into detailed time-series data on the compositional characteristics of encounters, which was collected with explicit participant consent. Additional behavioral shifts, including a heightened aversion to exploring new places and modified visitation propensity models, account for much of the long-term drop in diversity. These insights can guide the formulation of pandemic exit strategies aimed at minimizing permanent reductions in urban interaction diversity.

The simulations reveal an unexpected phenomenon termed the \emph{curvature effect}, signifying a pronounced asymmetric geometric deformation within the parametric space triggered by substantial fluctuations in the system's entropy. This asymmetric pattern is linked to the onset of hysteresis, thereby establishing an intrinsic arrow of time within the system's dynamics. This finding provides a novel, unified perspective on the physical mechanisms driving symmetry breaking and the emergence of the arrow of time during nonequilibrium phase transitions. Furthermore, this approach offers a powerful, generalizable framework for investigating physical phenomena previously lacked by current theoretical models. (Physical Review E 101, 062115, 2020)

$\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA), a robust alternative to conventional PCA, has gained significant popularity in recent years. This study examines a rotationally invariant variant of L1-PCA, which remains largely unexplored in existing literature. To address this challenge, we introduce a proximal alternating linearized minimization method incorporating nonlinear extrapolation to solve the problem's two-block reformulation. We further demonstrate that the proposed algorithm converges at least linearly to a limiting critical point of the reformulated problem, which is proven to correspond to a critical point of the original problem provided a specific step size condition is met. Finally, numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate our theoretical findings and illustrate the effectiveness of our approach.

However, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing (NLP) models possess embedded linguistic knowledge that can guide the annotation workflow. This study leverages the BERT neural language model to reintegrate information into an annotation task focused on semantically labeling dialog behaviors within "Emotion Twenty Questions" (EMO20Q), a question-asking game. We begin by outlining the background of BERT, the EMO20Q dataset, and assisted annotation processes, followed by a description of the methods used to fine-tune BERT for verifying annotated labels. Specifically, we employ a paraphrase task to ensure that all utterances sharing the same label are correctly identified as paraphrases of one another. We demonstrate that this approach effectively assesses and revises annotations of complex, utterance-level semantic labels in textual user data. Furthermore, we show that this method can be readily adapted to apply to other annotated NLP labels. By validating the reuse of embedded linguistic knowledge in NLP models for supporting the annotation of large-scale social media data, our work facilitates the production of high-quality datasets. Consequently, this enables the training of more advanced ML models to better capture the semantic semantics of user-generated content.

robotics, with the map serving as the foundational element. While most existing map representations depend on drift-free state estimation to generate global metric maps, maintaining such consistency and speed is challenging in large-scale real-world scenarios. This paper introduces HiTMap, a novel representation designed to improve upon current methods. Its core concept involves utilizing a submap-based hierarchical topology instead of a global metric map, thereby maintaining only local metric maps for obstacle avoidance and ensuring the system remains lightweight. To facilitate exploration of unknown areas, frontiers are identified and integrated into the map as attributes. Furthermore, a path planning module was developed to assess the feasibility and efficiency of this representation. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated through both simulation and real-world testing, and the HiTMap implementation is released as open-source.

In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. Additionally, the proposed apparatus could directly measure the boundary between the superconducting and normal states on a thin-film sample, offering high sensitivity to minor variations in thickness, temperature, or doping levels that affect the critical current. Furthermore, given that the expelled magnetic field near a thin-film superconductor can reach the upper critical field of type-II superconductors, this method holds potential for determining that critical parameter. To demonstrate the feasibility of these proposals, numerical simulations of atomic interference patterns under the influence of magnetic field gradients were conducted.

viewed as inefficient for SIMD high-performance computing (HPC), even though many critical HPC applications naturally possess an object-based structure. On SIMD accelerators like GPUs, this limitation stems primarily from memory allocation and access issues. Although a few libraries offer parallel memory allocation for accelerator devices, they all suffer from uncoalesced memory accesses.

We have identified a broad category of object-oriented programs, including many significant real-world applications, that can be efficiently executed on massively parallel SIMD accelerators. We term this category Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), as it expresses parallelism by executing a specific method across all instances of a given type.

To enable average programmers to utilize fast GPU programming for SMMO applications, we developed DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework. DynaSOAr comprises three core components: (1) a fully parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator; (2) a data layout Domain-Specific Language (DSL); and (3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. By controlling both memory allocation and access, DynaSOAr outperforms state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators.

DynaSOAr enhances memory utilization by adopting a Structure of Arrays (SoA) data layout and reduces memory fragmentation through the efficient management of free and allocated blocks using lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps. Unlike other allocators, our design relies heavily on atomic operations, prioritizing overall application performance over individual kernel runtime optimization.

To ensure coalesced memory access, the language maps the conventional for-loop construct to the parallel do-all operation. This results in contiguous memory access, minimized global memory traffic, and reduced kernel occupancy. We implemented this mapping using a transformation based on CUDA functional primitives.

Our evaluation on various single and multi-kernel SMMO applications demonstrates that DynaSOAr achieves near-peak GPU throughput for kernel execution and exhibits superior memory utilization and fragmentation management compared to existing libraries. Furthermore, by leveraging a straightforward, portable, and high-level API, developers can achieve near-peak GPU throughput with minimal code adaptation when running SMMO applications on current and future accelerators.

Through a detailed orbital decomposition of local densities of states, we examine the formation mechanisms of YSR states for an Mn adatom and two configurations of Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface, contrasting our theoretical outcomes with recent experimental data. For the adatom, our findings indicate that spin-orbit coupling causes minor shifts in certain YSR peaks, while local spin-polarization on Nb atoms has negligible influence on their positions. Furthermore, scaling the exchange field at the Mn site accounts for the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum. Our results for a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer align well with the experimentally observed splitting of YSR states; however, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, the spin-orbit coupling proves insufficient to explain the experimentally observed splitting. Additionally, altering the relative orientation of magnetic moments within this dimer induces splitting and energy shifts of the YSR states, ultimately resulting in the emergence of a new state at zero energy. We contend that this new YSR state arises from the subgap states associated with a midgap impurity state, which originates from a distortion in the Nb adatom orbitals induced by the exchange interaction between Mn atoms. Finally, we discuss the significance of our conclusions for interpreting recent experimental observations of YSR states involving multiple energy scales. An accompanying video offers a visual representation of the orbitals constituting the YSR states for various Mn dimers.

This paper addresses the question of determining the maximum value of $\lambda$ such that any 2-edge-coloring of the complete graph on $\mathbb{N}$ guarantees a monochromatic infinite $F$-factor with a vertex set possessing an upper density of at least $\lambda$, for a given finite graph $F$. We establish a novel lower bound for this problem; for specific graphs $F$, including cliques and odd cycles, this bound is optimal as it aligns with a previously known upper bound. Furthermore, in the specific instance where $F$ is a triangle, we provide an explicit lower bound of $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \approx 0.62203$, which surpasses the earlier best result of $3/5$. This study utilizes QED particle-in-cell simulations that incorporate electron-positron spin and photon polarization to examine a standard laser-solid configuration where an ultraintense linearly polarized laser strikes a foil target featuring a micrometer-scale preplasma. Our results indicate that when laser intensity surpasses $10^{24}~\rm W/\rm cm^2$ and positron yield becomes significant, the produced positrons exhibit clear polarization. Specifically, these polarized positrons can achieve a polarization degree exceeding 30% and a charge greater than 30 nC, with a flux of $10^{12}\,{\rm sr}^{-1}$. This angular dependence stems from the asymmetrical laser fields experienced by positrons within the skin layer of the overdense plasma, where radiative spin-flip and radiation reaction are critical factors. for dense thermal monitoring in systems on chip that support dynamic voltage and frequency scaling. The sensor's front-end utilizes a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to transform local temperature into two biasing currents, which subsequently determine two oscillation frequencies. The ratio of these frequencies corresponds directly to the absolute temperature. The back-end then converts this frequency ratio into a digital temperature code. Benefiting from its low-complexity architecture, the design offers a compact footprint, low power usage, and high accuracy across a broad temperature spectrum. Additionally, an embedded line regulation mechanism enables voltage scalability. Prototyped in 180nm CMOS, the sensor operates within a 0°C to 100°C detection range, supports a supply voltage from 0.6V to 1.8V, and occupies a minimal silicon area of 0.021mm². Experimental results from 20 test chips demonstrate competitive performance metrics, including a resolution of 0.25°C, an inaccuracy of ±1.5°C, a sampling rate exceeding 200Hz, and an energy consumption of approximately 1.26nJ per conversion at 30°C. Statistical tests reveal that protostellar cores possess greater mass than starless cores, even when accounting for biases related to temperature and opacity. We propose that this mass disparity signifies core growth occurring after formation. Consequently, massive star formation may not necessarily originate from massive prestellar cores, contingent upon the rate of this mass accretion. The implications of this finding for the relationship between the core mass function and the stellar initial mass function require further investigation. Additionally, the average mass of our protostellar cores is approximately 2 times the local Jeans mass; cores with masses below this threshold likely cannot form stars. This supports the notion that there is no minimum mass requirement for star formation, nor does it imply that very low-mass cores are simply underrepresented in molecular clouds. Ultimately, the physics governing low-mass cores differs significantly from that of massive cores, suggesting that enhancing the star formation efficiency of existing low-mass cores (around 20%) could potentially accelerate the formation of massive stars within molecular clouds.

Specifically, for the sphere ${\mathbb S}^{d-1} \subset {\mathbb R}^d$, the strict positive definiteness of a zonal function $f(\cos \theta)$ is governed by the signs of the coefficients in its expansion using Gegenbauer polynomials $\{C^\lambda_n\}$, where $\lambda=(d-2)/2$. While recent work has classified such functions for specific ranges of $\lambda$, a comprehensive classification for all $\lambda>0$ remains elusive due to the difficulty in explicitly determining the dimension of the cone of positive definite zonal functions, denoted ${\cal K}^\lambda_{d-1}$. This paper introduces a new algorithm to approximately compute this dimension, yielding an explicit description of the dimension of ${\cal K}^\lambda_{d-1}$ and, consequently, a complete classification of positive definite zonal functions on ${\mathbb S}^{d-1}$. The proposed algorithm was executed for $0<\lambda\le 50$ in steps of $0.01$, with results indicating that the dimension of ${\cal K}^\lambda_{d-1}$ is typically either $\lfloor 2\lambda+2 \rfloor$ or $\lfloor 2\lambda+2 \rfloor -1$. Furthermore, findings regarding the dimension of ${\cal K}^\lambda_{d-1}$ have implications for the Legendre conjecture. Additionally, the results extend to zonal functions, demonstrating that a zonal function is strictly positive definite when its expansion consists of $\lambda$-positive sequences.

We anticipate this facility will detect light Dirac DM interacting via the photon, with a cross section and mass consistent with the p4n anomaly. The precision achieved at the STC will significantly advance our understanding of light DM properties, such as neutral current interactions and polarizability, following discovery. The STC may also reveal DM that is completely blind to photons. These invisible decays are notably clean from hadonic final state uncertainties, making the STC an ideal platform to investigate potential anomalies from LHC experiments and direct detection surveys. Abstract/Background: This study develops MFSSA to improve upon existing techniques for analyzing and forecasting functional time series (FTS) by integrating Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (MSSA) with functional principal component scores. Although MSSA was created for multivariate data, its direct application to FTS often underperforms compared to other algorithms. However, we show that MSSA is effective for multivariate data when appropriate lags are selected, and we introduce a method to optimize these lags using the Generalized Distance Function (GDF). Furthermore, the R package RfssA implements MFSSA, facilitating its application to various datasets. Although MFSSA is primarily intended for predictive analysis of FTS, it can also be utilized to examine the spectral characteristics of such data.

Recent advancements in measurement technology have enabled the efficient collection of functional time series (fts), which represent curves, surfaces, or other multivariate functions observed over time. Despite this, no comprehensive methodology currently exists to analyze such data. To address this gap, we propose MFSSA, a new approach that merges Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (MSSA) with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to analyze and forecast fts. The R package RfssA makes MFSSA applicable to various types of functional data. Simulations and two empirical studies demonstrate that MFSSA outperforms existing methods in both reconstruction and forecasting tasks. MFSSA can be extended to handle missing data and is potentially applicable to other multivariate forecasting problems. Keywords: Multivariate singular spectrum analysis, functional data analysis, time series analysis, signal extraction, forecasting, R package. In this expression, $\phi(x,b) = \mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$, where the parameter $\kappa(x,b)$ is given by $\frac{\sqrt{1-x}|b|}{\sqrt{1-x}+x|b|}$ and is nearly proportional to the distance from $x$ to the boundary $1$. The coefficient b(t,x) = $\frac{1}{t\sigma^2} \sum_{s=1}^t (\rho_s^2-1)$ captures the time-averaged squared projection of the increments onto the unit sphere, with $\rho_s$ representing the ratio of the discrete to continuous noise variances in a typical simulation of the reflection principle; consequently, b depends on the specific dynamics of the walk. The function $\phi(x,b)$ can be approximated quadratically for small $1-x$ and $|b|$, and numerically for general $x$ and $b$. This result elucidates previously observed power-law decay rates in similar contexts, offering insights into their varying exponents and providing exact decay laws for finite times. The proposed dynamic generalization of the exponent $\beta$ represents a significant advancement over previous approximations, which either assumed uniform distribution of the projected increments (yielding $b=0$) or ignored their correlation with time $t$ (resulting in $b=0$). The theoretical findings are validated against direct simulations. The core methodology relies on an exact recursive equation for $p(t,x)$, which can be approximately solved for large $t$ using continuous functions that capture the typical behavior of the underlying stochastic process. The specialized case $x=0$ is examined in detail. Mathematical expectations conditionally on non-extinction are analyzed. The derivation of the recursive equation and its transformation into an integral equation are described. Additionally, connections to similar problems arising in financial mathematics are explored. (IShTAR) serves as a specialized facility at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Garching, Germany, designed to study the interaction between ICRF waves and plasma. A plasma source, measuring 0.1 meters in length and 0.4 meters in diameter, generates the required plasma environment ahead of the ICRF antenna. This source, which features a helical antenna, was engineered to achieve a helicon discharge mode. Although it was previously unconfirmed whether the source could reach this mode, achieving helicon operation is crucial for maximizing the source's capacity and producing high-density plasma. Consequently, a comprehensive study was conducted to attain helicon mode. This involved characterizing key plasma parameters—such as electron temperature, density, and plasma potential—and implementing a global model for particle and power balance. The study confirmed the existence of helicon mode at magnetic fields below 35 mT. To achieve the maximum possible plasma density, an optimization strategy was proposed to enable helicon mode operation at the highest available magnetic field. Upon successful implementation of this strategy, the source is anticipated to yield significantly higher plasma densities, thereby enhancing the facility's overall performance.

Nucleus segmentation technology is commonly employed to automate these tasks; however, training robust segmentation models remains challenging due to issues like nucleus adhesion, stacking, and excessive background fusion. Although recent approaches based on point annotation have significantly enhanced model performance, they still require experienced pathologists to provide the necessary annotations. To leverage the benefits of point-annotation-based methods while reducing manual workload and improving the efficiency and accuracy of cancer diagnosis, an automatic nucleus detection algorithm is needed to efficiently locate nuclei and extract valuable information from pathological images. This paper introduces a W-shaped network for automatic nucleus detection. Unlike traditional U-Net-based methods that directly map pathology images to target masks, our approach decomposes the detection task into two sub-tasks: first mapping the original image to a binary mask, and then mapping that binary mask to a density mask. Experimental results on the BCDD dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, yielding three key findings: (1) the W-shaped network effectively improves automatic nucleus detection; (2) splitting tasks into binary mask and density mask detection optimizes overall performance; and (3) the use of point annotations yields superior results compared to mask annotations. To address this, recent models have been developed to function in non-Euclidean spaces, particularly hyperbolic geometry. Although hyperbolic GCNs demonstrate promising results, current hyperbolic graph operations fail to strictly adhere to hyperbolic geometry, potentially limiting the space's utility and degrading model performance. Furthermore, we observe that replacing standard graph operations with those defined in this paper can enhance the performance of certain existing hyperbolic GCNs. To our knowledge, this work is the first to systematically rebuild hyperbolic graph operations using Lorentzian geometry, offering a theoretical foundation for the reliable learning of representations in hyperbolic space. This perspective provides a physical justification for covariant harmonic gauges, which arise when a mass term is introduced for the gravitational perturbation. Specifically, selecting a particular harmonic gauge yields a theory of linearized massive gravity with the expected five degrees of freedom, successfully avoiding the vDVZ discontinuity that plagues the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. Furthermore, this framework offers an efficient method for calculating propagators in various dimensional backgrounds, as the parameter dependence allows for the derivation of massless propagators from massive ones. Consequently, we recover the standard Feynman propagator in four dimensions and discover a novel harmonic gauge that yields the propagator in any arbitrary dimension. These findings are particularly significant for approaches to quantum gravity based on AdS/CFT correspondence and asymptotically AdS spacetimes, including recent advancements on the vDVZ discontinuity in the semi-classical limit of three-dimensional AdS space. Our results confirm previous findings regarding the absence of this discontinuity in four-dimensional AdS space and facilitate the investigation of such phenomena in higher dimensions.

Although GANs have proven effective in creating and altering natural images, their use within the medical field remains nascent. By leveraging the CheXpert dataset, we demonstrate that StyleGAN can be trained to produce authentic chest X-rays. Drawing inspiration from the Cyclic Reverse Generator (CRG) framework, we developed an encoder capable of accurately inverting the generator for synthetic X-rays and reconstructing real images at the organ level. The tool incorporates various statistical techniques, including standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA), elastic maps (a non-linear PCA variant), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), multilinear regression, K-Means clustering, and a decision tree algorithm variant. Featuring intuitive interfaces for customizing the position and scale of data clouds (clusters) formed by objects, ViDaExpert utilizes these 2D representations for analytical data work. As its name implies, the system is designed to function as a virtual reality environment, employing head-mounted displays and hand controllers to enable users to navigate and manipulate data clouds in an immersive 3D space. Additionally, it includes a free-view camera mode that allows users to explore recorded stereoscopic video footage of data clouds generated by Expert systems. To better illustrate the system's capabilities, this paper presents a demo video. ViDaExpert represents a innovative approach to free-view stereoscopic visualization that facilitates the analysis of standard statistical methods for high-dimensional data. The associated video provides a more thorough system overview, including a free-view camera mode for navigating recorded ViDaExpert sessions with experts, hand tracking support, and a higher-resolution data set.
